item.title: Magic Mushrooms, Mental Health, and the $1,900 "Trip"
item.description:
Psychedelics

Magic Mushrooms, Mental Health, and the $1,900 "Trip"

Is psilocybin therapy ready for prime time? New studies find benefits and risks.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Oregon's psilocybin centers show encouraging safety practices, but screening is not a psychiatric evaluation.
  • A memorable psychedelic experience does not necessarily mean lasting improvement in depression or addiction.
  • Serious adverse reactions and gaps in reporting highlight the need for long-term monitoring and follow-up.
  • Psilocybin's future lies in standardized pharmaceuticals with proven safety and efficacy, not just the trip.

Could I call an Oregon psilocybin center, buy magic mushrooms, take them home, and party? Would anyone ask about my bipolar disorder, drug use, thoughts of suicide, or if I take antidepressants? Or would this be marijuana dispensaries all over again, but with a more interesting afternoon ahead?

The VA is already preparing for possible FDA-approved psychedelic treatments for PTSD and depression. And as many as 2.1 million veterans could potentially benefit. FDA approval is one hurdle. Delivering safe, effective psychiatric care is another.

Using a familiar consumer-protection technique, Washington University in St. Louis investigators, secret shoppers or prospective customers, asked licensed psilocybin centers about eligibility, safety, and costs. Their findings, published October 12, 2026, were reassuring—but not a clean bill of health. WashU’s Kevin Xu, M.D., MPH, expected something closer to a dispensary model, with minimal screening and extravagant therapeutic claims. Instead, staff actually did ask about psychiatric history, medications, and risk factors.

They found that no centers offered take-home psilocybin. They also did not offer immediate administration without further screening. Fourteen disclosed that psilocybin could not be given to patients who were taking lithium due to contraindications. All the centers at least addressed suicidal ideation through at least one information channel.

Encouraging. But investigators evaluated what callers were told—not what actually happens during dosing, whether screening was adequate, or what happened afterward.

I’ve spent much of my career watching promising psychoactive drugs move from the research bench to the patient’s bedside. Many questions remain: Are these psychiatric treatments or supervised psychedelic experiences?

Another observational study followed 346 adults receiving Oregon’s regulated psilocybin services. At one month, 92.2 percent reported benefiting. By three months, participants reported improvements in depression, anxiety, PTSD symptoms, well-being, and life satisfaction—no placebo or comparison group. Expectations, preparation, psychological support, and setting may have contributed. Association is not causation.

Four participants (1.2 percent), all of them psychedelic-naive, experienced serious psilocybin reactions requiring medical attention. One had a violent reaction requiring hospital transport. Another subsequently reported worsening depression and anxiety, emergency care, and new thoughts about death or self-harm.

Alarmingly, only one of these four events appeared in the facilitator-reporting system.

Who is responsible after the trip?

Oregon Is Not a Mushroom Dispensary

Since 2023, Oregon has licensed psilocybin services. Clients must be at least 21, complete preparation, and consume psilocybin under supervision at a licensed center—no take-home mushrooms.

But here’s the distinction that interests me most: No psychiatric diagnosis, prescription, or physician referrals. Neither evaluators nor facilitators need to be psychiatrists, psychologists, or mental health professionals.

They cannot screen, diagnose, or treat psychiatric disorders within this system.

A screening questionnaire is just that. It is not a psychiatric examination by a trained professional. Asking about suicidal thoughts is not a suicide risk assessment.

A checklist is no substitute for professional training, clinical experience, and judgment, particularly with unstable psychiatric illness, multiple medications, or a history of addiction.

What is being offered? A supervised psychedelic experience. Not necessarily psychiatric treatment.

Magic Mushrooms vs Psilocybin

This seems like a no-brainer. Imagine prescribing foxglove leaves for heart failure, testing a sample, and hoping every dose contains the right amount of cardiac medicine. Modern medicine moved from foxglove to standardized pharmaceuticals like digoxin for many good reasons—dose and safety matter.

Plants to Purified Medicines
Source: Mark Gold, M.D., used with permission

Oregon requires laboratory potency, content, and labeling to identify both psilocybin and psilocin. But testing a mushroom batch is not the same as manufacturing a pure pharmaceutical with validated dose-uniformity, purity, and consistency. Natural products vary.

Research trial investigators use purified, research-grade psilocybin. This lets them standardize dosing, evaluate adverse events, and measure improvement in specific psychiatric disorders in controlled research trials.

Demonstrating safety and efficacy for FDA approval requires more than a memorable experience. We look for rigorous trials, reproducible results, and long-term follow-up.

Clinical investigators use purified, research-grade psilocybin to standardize dosing in rigorous trials. They can then reliably evaluate adverse events, measure improvement in specific psychiatric disorders, and conduct long-term follow-up.

Nature gave us the poppy, coca leaf, and other plant medicines. Modern evidence-based medicine has learned to reduce risks and increase response rates through pharmaceutical purification and measurement of dose and response. Psilocybin deserves the same discipline.

Nature's Pipeline of New Medications
Source: Mark Gold, MD, with permission

Depression Is Not Always Depression

Depression may be unipolar, bipolar, caused by another illness, or due to drug effects. Even treatment-resistant depression (TRD) may be misdiagnosed as bipolar disorder.

Lithium combined with psychedelics, including psilocybin, has been associated with seizures and is generally contraindicated. Patients should never discontinue psychiatric medications without consulting their prescribers.

Psilocybin research is promising. But screening is not diagnosis, and Oregon’s supervised psychedelic experiences are not FDA-approved psychiatric treatments.

From Nature to Pharmaceutical Medicine

Nature gave us willow bark, digitalis, morphine, and penicillin. Why should psilocybin be different?

On October 21, 2026, the Institute for Clinical and Economic Review (ICER) announced an evaluation of COMP360, synthetic psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (TRD), comparing its clinical and economic value with esketamine, IV ketamine, and TMS. Encouraging. But evaluation is not FDA approval.

On October 26, the National Law Review reviewed FDA officials’ position on psychedelic drug development. The FDA recognizes difficulties with blinded trials but still requires meaningful, durable benefits and safety monitoring. A remarkable trip is not an FDA endpoint.

Remember MDMA for PTSD? In 2024, promising results failed to secure FDA approval. Evidence matters.

Could future psychedelics retain therapeutic benefits without prolonged hallucinations and hours of supervision? Perhaps. An important research question. Not yet an established treatment.

The $1,900 Question

Are we developing an intervention for people with serious psychiatric illness—or an expensive, potentially meaningful experience for people who can afford it?

In the OPEN cohort, 29 percent of participants with reported income data earned more than $200,000, and over three-quarters had completed college. The median quoted session price in the mystery-shopper study was approximately $1,900. No center accepted insurance.

An Encouraging Beginning, Not the Final Answer

Oregon is conducting an important experiment. The OPEN cohort reported major benefits. At one month, nearly 59 percent ranked their psilocybin experience among the 10 most meaningful of their lives.

Meaningful? Certainly. But is meaningful the same as therapeutic?

Not necessarily. An awe-inspiring, psychologically memorable experience does not establish lasting improvement in depression. We need to measure outcomes, not memories.

The OPEN cohort also identified four serious behavioral reactions. Only one of the four serious behavioral reactions appeared in the facilitator-reporting system. Oregon operates outside conventional psychiatric treatment, and complications emerging weeks or months later may go unrecognized.

At three months, 8.7 percent reported symptoms suggestive of hallucinogen-persisting perception disorder (HPPD), although most reported little distress. Persistent perceptual changes deserve longer follow-up, even when they do not meet diagnostic criteria for HPPD.

Why not have independent safety monitoring, reliable adverse-event reporting, access to qualified clinicians, and follow-up at six months, one year, and beyond?

An FDA-approved psilocybin medicine would offer standardized dosing, pharmaceutical manufacturing, and controlled evidence of safety and efficacy for specific disorders. It wouldn’t eliminate risks, but it would provide a more rigorous basis for treatment.

The mushroom is the beginning of the story. Not necessarily the final product.

item.title: Why a Healthy Lifestyle Can’t Fix Loneliness
item.description:
Loneliness

Why a Healthy Lifestyle Can’t Fix Loneliness

Being busy isn’t the same as being connected. Research shows why it matters.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Research confirms you can be busy but still feel lonely and disconnected.
  • A healthy lifestyle may buffer the effects of loneliness, but not the feeling of disconnection.
  • Lonely, isolated women may lose 2.4 years free of physical disease; for men, the numbers are different.
  • Fewer but stronger connections may be better for you than a jam-packed calendar.
Source: Aaron Burden / Unsplash

One of my favorite films to rewatch in moments when I need some comfort is Up. Pixar’s tale of grief, aging, connection, and adventure brings tears to my eyes every single time. Loss can bring a sense of discombobulation that can challenge who we are and how we see ourselves. Anyone who has lost a loved one knows this. But it doesn’t have to be the loss of a person that brings us to feel alone. Retirement, becoming empty nesters, or even just a changing sense of self can alter how connected we feel with the world around us. How do these changes impact our physical and mental health?

“Our language has wisely sensed these two sides of man’s being alone. It has created the word 'loneliness' to express the pain of being alone. And it has created the word 'solitude' to express the glory of being alone.” ― Paul Tillich, The Eternal Now

A study published in Nature Communications by researchers at Tulane University decided to look at exactly this. Looking at 277,489 adults aged 40 to 69 from the UK Biobank, all of whom started out free of seven major chronic conditions, they wanted to try to ascertain how feeling alone vs. social contact impacted both physical and mental health.

For the purposes of their research, the authors defined ‘Social isolation as an objective measure of the amount of social connection a person has, while loneliness is a subjective measure of a person’s dissatisfaction with the quality of their relationships—regardless of how social the person actually is.’ Is having a diary full of activities and meetings the same as feeling connected to others? It’s an important question to ask as the culture of busyness and hustle thrives in our social media-driven worlds. Using an observational design, the researchers decided to measure outcomes by looking at how many years people aged 50 and up could expect to live free of disease.

The researchers compared people who were both lonely and isolated with those who were neither. Considering physical conditions first, the researchers found that women who were both lonely and isolated lost 2.4 years free of physical disease vs. men losing 1.7 years. When it came to mental health, things looked slightly different. Women lost around 3.7 years free of mental disorders, and men nearly six.

When it comes to lifestyle interventions, it can be really hard to differentiate the impacts of individual lifestyle factors. In reality, many people take on changes in lifestyle habits in multiples. Exercising more, going to bed early, and cutting back on alcohol often form a triad of both advice offered and habits adopted. Here, the team found that having a healthy lifestyle (good diet, exercise, decent sleep, not smoking) helped buffer the effects of isolation, but made no meaningful difference to loneliness.

My understanding of this research mirrors what I’ve seen play out in practice. You can do everything right on paper but still feel lonely. This feeling of disconnection is often reported in younger people and adults who may have a very active online presence. The Biobank study is an observational study, so it can’t prove loneliness causes illness, but it does suggest that how connected we feel needs to be taken as seriously as our step count.

Back in the early 2000s, I remember chatting with a friend who was stuck in one of those dramatic relationships that you can only have in your 20s. You know the ones; when it’s clearly going nowhere, one day it’s on, the next it’s off, but yet the elastic band that is holding you together still can’t be snapped. “I hate the thought of being on my own,” she told me tearfully, over our chardonnay, “but my mother keeps telling me that there is nothing lonelier than being with the wrong person.”

Their relationship finally ended, but those words have stuck with me ever since. Being alone and feeling lonely are not the same thing. We’ve seen in our favorite characters—Fleabag, Bridget Jones, and Ted Lasso—that you can be surrounded by people at work, socially, even at home and still feel desperately alone.

Living with a chronic illness, I’m aware my life has become smaller. An introvert at heart, when I read these findings, it made me pause and think about how connected I really feel. And I believe taking an inventory of this is a really important place to start.

Here are the questions I asked myself:

  • In the workplace, how connected do I feel, both within my professional role and to my colleagues?

  • In friendships and casual coffees, who am I spending my time with, and how connected to both them and myself do I feel before, during, and after?

  • How frequently am I meeting people outside of my immediate circle? How do I feel about that?

I found it really illuminating, and I’ve made some changes to my personal and professional life as a result. Moving through life stages brings both challenges and opportunities in both the frequency of social contacts and how connected we feel, and it’s important we consider our own relationship with these.

How to improve

Identifying where your weaker spots are is important. Getting out and meeting people can feel intimidating for different reasons at different stages of life, but treating it as an important lifestyle factor, like sleep, nutrition, and diet, can help.

As the study suggests, having a healthier lifestyle overall can help mitigate the effects of isolation. Feeling lonely can be harder to deal with. If it’s something that is swamping your life or having a serious impact on your ability to function, it’s important to discuss it with your doctor.

But otherwise it might be more of a tweak in how you spend your time. Less may be more. Instead of seeing friends who leave you feeling uplifted and heard just once a year, it might be worth finding a way to add a second meet-up. Similarly, the weekly coffee with a nearby friend that leaves you feeling stressed or frustrated might be worth swapping for a trip to the gym, or something else that gives you more back.

And if you need a quick reminder of how connections can be found in the most unexpected places, there is always Up.

item.title: Hundreds of Suicide Victims Could Be Alive Today
item.description:
Suicide

Hundreds of Suicide Victims Could Be Alive Today

The Barriers to Suicide Act will save lives.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Jumping deaths—as opposed to firearm deaths and overdose deaths—are relatively easy to prevent.
  • The suicide prevention net on the Golden Gate Bridge has led to new bipartisan legislation.
  • The Barriers to Suicide Act would fund physical suicide barriers at other jump sites.

Now that a net on the Golden Gate Bridge has proven to prevent suicides, bipartisan federal legislation has been introduced that would provide funding for suicide barriers—a tall railing or a net—at other jump sites in the U.S. The legislation has flaws, but the intent is meaningful. If the bill passes, other communities with jump sites won’t have to wait until more than 2,000 people have died—as they have at the Golden Gate Bridge—before a physical suicide deterrent is erected.

In September, senators Alex Padilla and Thom Tillis introduced the bipartisan Barriers to Suicide Act. It would create a competitive grant process for local and state governments to apply for funding to install tall railings or nets at jump sites, and fund a study to assess ways to reduce such deaths.[1]

“Too many Americans die by suicide, and we know physical barriers can help save lives during times of crisis,” Padilla said in a statement that touted the effectiveness of the Golden Gate Bridge suicide prevention net. “The Barriers to Suicide Act is commonsense, life-saving legislation that will help enhance safety standards and make our public infrastructure safer.”[2]

When he heard about The Barriers to Suicide Act, former Marin County coroner Ken Holmes was pleased but also wistful. During most of his four decades in office, Holmes and his staff were responsible for handling the bodies of Golden Gate Bridge suicides, and he saw firsthand the physical impact on victims and the emotional impact on families. “If only they had listened to us 20 years ago,” he lamented. [3]

By “us” he meant several people who advocated for a barrier early on; later, many others joined them. By “they” he meant the Golden Gate Bridge District board, San Francisco supervisors, former mayor Gavin Newsom, and other elected officials, the majority of whom were slow to embrace the addition of a physical suicide deterrent on San Francisco’s world-famous span.

Is a physical suicide barrier at all or nearly all jump sites—tall bridges, buildings, parking structures, freeway overpasses, cliffs, train crossings, and elsewhere—the answer to preventing suicides? Obviously not, since the majority of suicides are with a firearm, and secondarily by overdosing. Jumps account for fewer than 5 percent of all suicide deaths. Nevertheless, jumping deaths—as opposed to firearm deaths and overdoses—are relatively easy to prevent. A physical barrier ends the problem. With guns and pills, it’s more difficult. The prevalence of firearms and drugs, the ease with which they can be procured, and the opposition to any legislation by various industries that limits access make getting a bill passed nearly impossible.

If the net on the Golden Gate Bridge had been in place 20 years ago, roughly 500 people probably would still be alive today. It’s too late for them, but not for many others. That’s the point of the Barriers to Suicide Act.

item.title: Becoming Dada: What Draws a Father In
item.description:
Parenting

Becoming Dada: What Draws a Father In

A neuroscientist asks what pulls a father into caring for his toddler.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • New fathers show stronger reward-circuit responses to infant cues.
  • Fathers' oxytocin varies with how they interact with their infants.
  • Fathers' brains respond more strongly to their own infant than to an unfamiliar one.

This post is Part 1 in a two-part series.

When my toddler son feels overwhelmed or upset, he almost always comes to me and says, “Tell me a story.”

I pick him up, settle him on my lap, and begin the way I always do: “Once upon a time, there was a smart, kind, happy little boy…” He may still be crying when I start, but by the time I reach “kind and happy,” he is catching his breath and staring up at me. The story that follows usually involves some of his favorite things to do: swimming, playing on the playground, or going on walks, and almost always animals. On the way to the swimming spot, a dog, a duck, and a pig might join in and help him into the water. Two or three minutes into our story, he has calmed down enough to go about his business.

This past year, I discovered a talent I never knew I had. Apparently, I am really good at improvised storytelling. I knew that fatherhood would bring me joy. What I did not expect was how much I would come to enjoy these moments. I have caught myself yearning for them. There is something deeply moving about being trusted with helping him settle.

Of course, storytime is only one of the many things we share. We go on walks and read together, and he absolutely loves being tossed into the air. The storytelling is simply one of the moments that stays with me.

All this has made me wonder what fatherhood has done to my own brain.

As a behavioral neuroendocrinologist, I study the relationship between hormones, the brain, and behavior. Leading up to his birth, I read extensively about changes that accompany pregnancy and motherhood, and there was plenty to learn, including significant shifts in hormones and in brain structure and function that extend well into the transition to motherhood [1]. It never occurred to me, though, to read about the changes I would go through myself as a father. Professional expertise, it turns out, does not prevent personal blind spots.

So, I started reading more about the science that might inform our little father-son ritual.

A child’s request: He asks

“Tell me a story” is a request that I have come to want and expect.

Neuroscientists use the word reward for how experiences acquire value and shape what we seek. Enjoying something and wanting more of it are related but not identical. I can feel delighted as my son settles, and separately find myself hoping for another chance to share those minutes.

A study by James Rilling and colleagues [2] offers a glimpse into how the brain’s response to infants changes. The researchers scanned the brains of men before and after they became fathers for the first time, alongside men who did not become fathers. After childbirth, the new fathers showed stronger activity in reward and motivation regions when a cue signaled a chance to see an infant’s picture. The comparison group showed no such increase. In other words, once these men became fathers, the prospect of seeing a baby engaged their reward circuitry more strongly, which echoes my own wish for another chance to share those minutes with my son.

Much of my own research uses animal models, so this is a natural place for me to dig deeper. A vole cannot tell us what fatherhood feels like, but it can help us understand what makes care possible. Prairie voles are an especially useful model because males help raise their young.

In one experiment, male prairie voles that had spent two weeks paired with a female groomed unfamiliar pups more than sexually inexperienced males did [3], so experience had changed how they responded to young. The paired males also had more of a particular dopamine receptor called D1 in their nucleus accumbens, a region involved in reward and motivation. When researchers blocked those receptors in the nucleus accumbens, the paired males spent less time grooming the pups [3]. Effectively, interfering with a dopamine signal in a reward-related brain region altered a specific act of care, suggesting that this signaling helps drive caregiving.

For me, the satisfaction of helping my son is part of what draws me back, even when it takes patience.

Physical comfort: I pick him up

The next part of our ritual is physical. I sit on the couch, cross my legs, and settle him on my lap, often while he is still crying.

This closeness makes me think about oxytocin, a hormone with many functions, including a role in social bonding [4]. Ruth Feldman and colleagues [5] observed parents during a 15-minute play-and-contact session with their four- to six-month-old infants. Fathers who engaged in more active physical contact and exploratory play showed an increase in salivary oxytocin afterward. Fathers who engaged in less did not.

Mothers in the same study showed a different pattern. Their oxytocin tracked affectionate touch, like caresses and soft kisses, rather than playful contact. Tossing my son into the air or tickling him silly is probably the closest match to the playful kind. Settling him on my lap for a story is the quiet counterpart.

A saliva sample cannot tell us what oxytocin is doing in the brain, and the study does not show that contact caused the response [5]. Still, it suggests that fathers’ oxytocin can vary with how they engage with their infants. When I pick up my son, I know that being together can change how he feels. But now I am increasingly curious about what it might be doing to me.

The power of ritual: I say the familiar words

Every story begins with the same sentence, and that sentence is part of what works. He knows what is coming. I know what will hold his attention, which is a familiar sentence and a voice that drops lower than usual. Once he settles, he stares up at me, enthralled, as the story continues.

Familiarity with one’s own child shows up in the father’s brain, too. Philip Newsome and colleagues [6] scanned 32 first-time fathers about eight months after childbirth. The fathers responded more strongly to videos of their own infants than to an unfamiliar infant, in brain regions involved in understanding others, emotional regulation, and reward. Fathers who had reported stronger bonding at three months later showed a stronger own-infant response in a region involved in interpreting other people’s internal states. This study links fathers’ closeness with their later brain responses to their own child.

That fits what the ritual feels like from the inside. The bond between me and my son grows through small, repeated, shared things.

But the story is only part of it. In Part 2, I look at what it takes to stay with him when the story is not enough, and at what that staying may be doing to a father’s brain.

item.title: Does Bed-Sharing Cause Anxiety? It's About Timing
item.description:
Child Development

Does Bed-Sharing Cause Anxiety? It's About Timing

A child's bed-sharing may offer clues about their well-being.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Bed-sharing during infancy was not linked to later anxiety or depression.
  • Children who began bed-sharing later showed a higher likelihood of anxiety.
  • Later-onset bed-sharing may signal emotional difficulties rather than cause them.

Many parents have shared a bed with their child at some point. Sometimes it's a deliberate choice. Other times, after a period of sleep difficulties, fears, nightmares, or life changes. Do you wonder whether bed-sharing might affect your child's mental health? Our new research offers reassuring, though nuanced, answers.

Parents often receive conflicting messages about children's sleep. Some are told that bed-sharing fosters closeness and security, while others worry it may encourage dependency or emotional difficulties. The reality may be more complex.

What We Already Knew About Bed-Sharing

Earlier, we examined whether bed-sharing during infancy was associated with children's later emotional well-being and attachment (Bilgin and Wolke, 2022; Bilgin and colleagues, 2024). Reassuringly, we found no evidence that bed-sharing in infancy was linked to poorer mental health outcomes in childhood or less secure attachment in infancy.

These findings challenged the common assumption that sharing a bed with an infant has important consequences for children's emotional development. Instead, they suggested that bed-sharing during infancy is often a normal part of family life and may reflect a variety of practical, cultural, and parenting considerations.

Yet one important question remained unanswered: Could bed-sharing mean different things depending on when it begins? A baby who routinely shares a parent's bed may not be experiencing the same challenges as a preschooler who suddenly starts seeking a parent's bed at night.

Our new study built on this work by asking a different question: Could the age at which bed-sharing begins matter?

Source: David Veksler/Unsplash

Why Timing Matters

To answer this question, we turned to data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children, a UK study that has followed thousands of families from pregnancy onward. We examined whether bed-sharing was associated with anxiety and depression across childhood and adolescence. Importantly, rather than asking whether children bed-shared, we looked at when bed-sharing began (Bilgin and Parsons, 2026).

The results painted a more nuanced picture than a simple yes-or-no answer.

Bed-sharing during infancy was not linked to an increased risk of anxiety or depression later in childhood or adolescence. Children who slept in their parents' bed at six months of age did not show elevated rates of emotional disorders years later.

However, a different pattern emerged for children who started bed-sharing after infancy, during toddlerhood (at 18 months) or early childhood (at 3.5 years). These children were more likely to experience anxiety disorders later on. Children who began bed-sharing at 18 months or 3.5 years had approximately three times greater odds of anxiety at age 8 compared with children who did not bed-share.

Does This Mean Bed-Sharing Causes Anxiety?

Probably not.

This is perhaps the most important message for parents.

Our findings do not suggest that bed-sharing itself causes anxiety. Bed-sharing that begins beyond infancy may signal that a child or family is already experiencing challenges. It may be better understood as a marker of underlying difficulties than as a cause.

Think of it this way: A child who suddenly wants to sleep in their parents' bed at age 3 may be experiencing worries, separation difficulties, nightmares, a period of stress, or sleep problems. The bed-sharing is not necessarily the problem. Instead, it may reflect other difficulties.

Children often communicate their needs through behaviour. When bed-sharing begins beyond infancy, it may indicate a child's emotional world rather than causing emotional difficulties itself.

Looking Beyond Sleep Arrangements

We also found that later-onset bed-sharing was more common among families experiencing other challenges, including:

  • Child sleep problems
  • Maternal mental health difficulties
  • Single-parent households
  • Social and economic disadvantage

This suggests that children's sleep arrangements do not occur in isolation. Instead, children's temperaments, sleep patterns, family well-being, and the wider circumstances in which families live can shape this.

For this reason, focusing solely on whether a child sleeps alone or with a parent may miss the bigger picture.

What Should Parents Do?

If your child occasionally sleeps in your bed, there is no reason to panic.

For many families, bed-sharing is a temporary response to illness, disrupted sleep, developmental transitions, or stressful life events.

Instead, consider the context:

  • Has your child recently become more fearful or anxious?
  • Have there been changes at home or school?
  • Is your child struggling with sleep, nightmares, or separation at bedtime?
  • Are there stresses affecting family well-being?

These questions may be more informative than the sleep arrangement itself.

If bed-sharing begins suddenly in toddlerhood or early childhood and persists because a child appears distressed or unable to sleep independently, it may be worth exploring the underlying reasons. Addressing the child's worries, sleep difficulties, or sources of stress may be more helpful than focusing on bed-sharing alone.

The Bigger Takeaway

Parenting discussions around bed-sharing are often framed as a debate between "good" and "bad" sleep practices. However, taken together with our previous studies on infant bed-sharing, the evidence points to a more nuanced conclusion.

Bed-sharing during infancy was not associated with poorer attachment relationships or later mental health difficulties. In contrast, bed-sharing that begins beyond infancy may reflect different developmental processes and family circumstances.

Rather than treating all bed-sharing as the same, researchers and parents may benefit from paying closer attention to when it occurs and why it begins.

For parents, the key question may not be, "Is bed-sharing harmful?" But rather, "Why is my child seeking extra closeness at night right now?"

Sometimes children's sleep behaviours tell us something important, not about where they sleep, but about what they may need from the people who care for them.

item.title: Would You Let Your House Keep an Eye on You?
item.description:
Caregiving

Would You Let Your House Keep an Eye on You?

Considering home monitoring technology to support independent living.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Home monitoring tools can provide solutions for safety concerns and forgotten tasks, like taking medications.
  • Cutting-edge tech being developed uses infrared sensors linked to AI—instead of cameras—to monitor the home.
  • Studies of age-tech report reassurance and feelings of safety, but also privacy and technical concerns.
Smart home age-tech ranges from the ordinary to almost sci-fi.
Source: JLco - Ana Suanes / iStock.com

My cousin once told me she worried that our grandma sometimes forgot to feed her dog, Bonnie. I suspected the opposite problem—that Bonnie was getting second dinners because she looked like a furry black-and-white soccer ball. Either way, it would have been nice to know whether Grandma’s routine was changing, for both her sake and Bonnie’s.

It turns out I’m not alone in wanting information that will help my loved ones—and myself—age in place. Most older adults want to stay in their own homes. However, some need intermittent or continuous monitoring for safety and well-being.

Age-tech, also called gerontechnology, might offer solutions.

Who Might Benefit from Age-Tech

Monitoring technology can be useful for adults with mild cognitive impairment or mild-to-moderate dementia—and even healthy older adults. (Is there anyone over 30 who has not left the stove on?)

Problems Age-Tech Can Solve—or Prevent

Age-tech that keeps an eye on the home can keep human and furry inhabitants safe or make their lives easier. There are many problems =age-tech can watch for—and sometimes fix or alert others to:

  • Forgotten tasks: Taking medications, taking out the garbage, making meals, or re-making meals for Grandma’s rotund dog.
  • Dangers: Doors left unlocked, wandering, falling, or hot appliances left on.
  • Inefficiencies and wasted money: Forgetting to adjust the heater or A/C or overwatering the yard (my friend’s mistaken overwatering caused a messy basement flood).

The High-Tech Solutions

Many people—of all ages—already use smartphones or wearables, such as smartwatches or rings, to track activity and health indicators. Some devices also track location using GPS.

But lesser-known monitoring tech is also available. Sensors on doors, cabinets, beds, and medication dispensers track behavior indirectly. These devices work by sensing pressure, movement, or magnetic contacts, or they use software applications.

Interior cameras provide another option. However, some people—and I count myself among them—don’t like the idea of video monitoring.

Some of the most fascinating advances involve passive monitoring by sensors, usually mounted on the ceiling. (The sensors for Washington State University’s (WSU’s) “Smart Home in a Box,” for example, can be installed in a few hours for research participants.)

The monitoring process is quite innovative. These aren’t videos; the sensors use passive sensing to detect changes in infrared radiation when someone moves around. Think of them like snakes on the ceiling, sensing infrared wavelengths as some snakes do when targeting prey. (Well, maybe don’t think of that if you don’t like snakes.)

The data just indicate activity in different locations over time. This affords greater privacy than video—there's no need to worry about walking around in your ratty old bathrobe.

Artificial intelligence (AI) software, often using machine learning, can recognize patterns and be designed to flag deviations from normal routines and notify others.

Imagine Aunt Freddy usually makes coffee at 7 a.m., but it’s 10 a.m. and no one has yet moved around the kitchen. The system could alert her neighbor or family.

There are important advantages to this kind of system. For instance, there is no need to charge a wearable device such as a smartwatch—or even put one on. That can be useful because some people simply don’t like wearing devices—or their partners object. My husband wears his smartwatch even when sleeping, and it lights up when he moves. On many a night, I’ve been rudely awakened by a tractor beam with the seeming light of a thousand suns.

What Monitoring Technology Can You Get Now

Some of these advanced research systems—such as AI-powered infrared monitoring kits—are not available to consumers yet. However, universities and organizations are working to make the technology more accessible. Maureen Schmitter-Edgecombe and Diane Cook—leading gerontechnology researchers at WSU—see this as an important goal.

But some of this impressive is available now. Lists of both high- and low-tech options can be found online from sources including university labs conducting research on age-tech or assistive technology, or the federally funded AT3 Center, which provides a directory of assistive technology programs in every U.S. state and territory.

How Do People Feel About Monitoring?

Research reveals both positive and negative reactions. A 2024 review reported on varied technologies used by pairs of older adults without cognitive impairment and their family caregivers, finding that those who used age-tech with monitoring functions generally rated them positively, reporting benefits such as greater feelings of safety and reduced stress. But they also noted challenges, including privacy concerns, technical problems, and mismatches with needs. Interestingly, in several studies, caregivers rated the technology more favorably than residents did.

For caregivers, it’s a good idea to start with a specific concern and discuss it with the potential user. What type of monitoring is useful for this person at this time? Is it for the home, person, or both?

Schmitter-Edgecombe offered this advice based on many years of gerontechnology research: As is true for most people, older adults are more open to new technology if they’ve had an experience that builds confidence, rather than frustration. In one study, when older adults first used an age-tech device successfully, they couldn’t wait to get their hands on other tech. I’d react the same way; a mastery experience is very motivating.

Second dinners!
Source: Snizhana Galytska / iStock.com

But if your smart home ever warns you not to give the dog a second dinner, Bonnie would recommend a second opinion.

Postscript: Ironically, while writing this post, I had a fall (tripped over luggage) and forgot to change a medication dosage. I’d better consider more age-tech myself.

For more on age-tech devices, see WSU’s Tech4Aging and its Center for Advanced Studies in Adaptive Systems.

item.title: The Hidden Benefits of Stress
item.description:
Stress

The Hidden Benefits of Stress

When we know what stress is, we can meet it with clear awareness and new skills.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Stress has been presented to us as a negative (and damaging) reaction to uncontrollable external forces.
  • But the word "stress" is a weasel word that hides the emotional nature of our stress response.
  • The emotions that make up our stress response exist for vital reasons, and we can learn how to work with them.
Source: Caroline Martins / Pexels

This post is Part 1 of a series.

In my book, The Language of Emotions, I focus on stress as a weasel word (a word we use to mask awareness) that hides emotions.

My work with emotions helps people unmask weasel words and identify the subtle emotional aspects of traits we generally don't see as emotions. For instance, motivation is an aspect of anxiety, while behavioral self-correction is an aspect of shame, and our capacity for fairness is an aspect of envy.

All of our emotions exist in many subtle levels of intensity that we've mostly learned to describe with weasel words.

Stress Is Our Most Overused Weasel Word for Emotions

What are you feeling when you're stressed? Are you angry or ashamed? Are you anxious or confused? Are you feeling panicky or embarrassed? What are you feeling?

"Stressed" is not a helpful answer to these questions because the way we've been taught to view stress leaves us with very few options except to calm ourselves down somehow. When we misidentify our emotions as stress, we disconnect ourselves from what's actually happening.

From The Language of Emotions:

The word "stress" doesn’t even come from the world of emotions; it comes from the world of physics and engineering, where it’s defined as a pressure, pull, or force exerted on one thing by another, or the internal resistance of a thing to the external forces applied to it. Interestingly, this word that refers to things—to inanimate objects—has found its way into our emotional vocabulary.

And our emotional definition of stress nearly equals the definition given to us by engineers; it has helped us view ourselves as objects being acted upon by forces instead of living, agile, and resourceful organisms. The word stress has become a universal catchall for emotions for people who don’t have a functional emotional vocabulary. Now if we’re sad, furious, frightened, exhilarated, exhausted, despondent, ashamed, mournful, panicky, or even suicidally depressed, we can use the word stress to describe our condition. This is not a sign of emotional awareness. (McLaren, 2023, p. 377)

Being able to identify and name our emotions is essential to our well-being. Dr. Lisa Feldman Barrett and her colleagues have found in study after study that having (or developing) a robust emotional vocabulary—all by itself—can help people develop stronger emotion regulation skills. Simply having more words for your emotions helps your brain and your body categorize them accurately and respond to them appropriately.

Which is why it's a shame that we aren't taught that our "stress" response is an emotional response. If we don't know what's happening inside us, we may not develop the skills we need to understand and regulate our necessary emotional responses to stressful situations.

But if we can learn how to identify and name the emotions that are hiding under the weasel word of stress, we can learn how to regulate them.

Uncovering the Emotional Vocabulary of Stress

In my applied work, I teach people to identify and name emotions, and then work with them directly instead of trying to repress, ignore, or exchange them for something else.

When I listen to people talk about stress, I see three emotions very clearly: anxiety (the emotion of motivation, task-completion, and deadline-awareness); panic (the emotion that steps forward when our lives are in danger); and anger (the emotion that helps us set and maintain boundaries around what we value).

Of course, other emotions can be involved, because each of our emotions contains intelligence and skills to help us navigate through the world, but these three are almost always present in our stress response.

Here are some simple ideas for engaging with these emotional responses to stressors:

Anxiety

  • Anxiety helps you organize, plan for, and complete your tasks and meet your deadlines. Stressors require some kind of action or plan, and anxiety brings you the focus and energy you need.
  • You work with your anxiety by intentionally marshalling your energy to help you focus on what needs to be done (list-making, for instance, is a specific anxiety-supporting skill).
  • The internal questions for anxiety are: What brought this feeling forward? What truly needs to be done?

Panic

  • Panic gives you the energy and instincts you need when you feel threatened or endangered. It's a fast-moving, fast-thinking emotion that relies on your instinctual survival skills.
  • You have four main choices during emergencies: Fight, flee, freeze, or flock to safety. Listen to your body – don’t think, just act. Your instinctual body is a survival expert, and it will keep you safe.
  • The internal questions for panic are: What is currently a threat? Please help me fight, flee, freeze, or flock to safety.

Anger

  • Anger helps you address challenges to what you value: your standpoint, your position, your interpersonal boundaries, or your self image. Your task is to restore these things without violating the boundaries of others.
  • Your anger may also step in when others are being challenged or devalued, and your task is to address the transgression and restore the boundaries of all parties.
  • The internal questions for anger are: What do I value? What must be protected and restored?

    From The Language of Emotions:

Stress in itself is not the problem; stress is a necessary and even sacred part of life. Without it, you would be untested, undifferentiated, unchallenged, and insufficiently resourced.

Even the word "stress" tells us this in an alternate definition, which is to underscore, accentuate, or emphasize something. When you feel stressed-out, you are in many ways slowing yourself down to notice, emphasize, and underscore (perhaps unconsciously) things that are deeply important to you. You don't stress over things you don't care about.

Stressors always uncover important issues; if you try to avoid stress or repress your stress responses, you won’t gain the agility you need to engage with the meaningful stressors of life in all their power and unpredictability. (McLaren, 2023, p. 380)

item.title: 'Falling' Back to Sleep
item.description:
Sleep

'Falling' Back to Sleep

How turning back the clocks affects our health.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Even a one hour time change can disrupt our circadian rhythm and affect mood and sleep.
  • The 'fall back' time change is generally easier to adjust to than the 'spring forward' time change.
  • Consistent sleep habits and morning daylight can help our bodies adjust to the fall time change.

As the fall months progress, I get excited for what’s to come—beautiful fall colours, crisp mornings, and anything pumpkin spice. But fall season also signals the end of daylight saving time—DST is the practice of moving clocks forward one hour in spring (spring forward) and back one hour in the fall (fall back). This practice was intended to make better use of natural daylight by shifting an hour of daylight from the early morning to the evening during the warmer months.

While it may seem like a small matter, this one-hour shift can throw off our body’s internal clock and disrupt sleep. In the days after the change, some individuals may experience measurable side effects. The good news is that the fall change is typically easier than the spring change, and simple light-timing and sleep basics can smooth the transition.

A brief history of Daylight Saving Time

The practice dates back to World War I. By adding an hour of evening light, the goal was more productive hours while also saving electricity and fuel. About 70 countries practice it, and it affects about a quarter of the world’s population. In many parts of the United States and Canada, changing the time twice a year is required, legally, despite ongoing debate about its utility. Critics have argued that the original energy-saving argument has not held up. Even the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends ridding the twice-yearly clock changes and keeping standard time.

The health impact of a one-hour time change

Our body runs on a tightly regulated 24-hour internal clock known as our circadian rhythm. The brain orchestrates this rhythm, and light is its most powerful timekeeper. When the clocks change, even by one hour, our circadian rhythm does not fall in line right away. For many of us, it can take several days to a couple of weeks to fully recalibrate, thus causing a temporary “circadian misalignment.” In a few cases, it can feel like mild jet lag from crossing one time zone. During this “circadian misalignment,” it’s not uncommon to have poor sleep quality the nights after the change, in addition to feelings of grogginess, fatigue, and diminished concentration. These symptoms are most pronounced when we lose one hour of sleep with the spring time change.

Is the fall time change harmful?

Thankfully, the fall time change is milder than the spring. For most of us, gaining an hour of sleep is much easier than losing one hour. Large studies have even suggested a small, short-term drop in heart problems and better mood afterward, likely from more morning daylight. But the “fall back” isn’t entirely harmless. Many are surprised to find they sleep a bit worse in the first week or two after the change, with difficulty falling or staying asleep being common, while others may experience a dip in mood as the evenings get dark earlier. I know I’m not alone in feeling a little down when I look outside at 4:30 pm, and it’s completely dark! Like you, there’s still so much of the day left to go. Thankfully, these effects are usually mild and resolve within a few days to weeks.

Your time-change toolkit

How can you prepare for the upcoming time change? The following simple steps will make it easier for your body and mind to adjust.

  1. Use light strategically

For the fall time change, get light in the late afternoon or early evening to help you stay awake. For example, a 30-minute walk after work or just before sunset may do the trick. Using light strategically during the day and early evenings will help delay your internal clock.

  1. Protect the basics of sleep

Stick to the sleep basics as much as possible. Keep a consistent bedtime and wake time as much as possible and minimize or avoid alcohol and caffeine around the transition since both disrupt sleep. Keep your bedroom dark, cool, and quiet; put away screens one hour before bed.

  1. Anticipate dips in mood

With the fall time change bringing earlier evenings quite suddenly, some may be prone to seasonal low mood, making it important to plan. Consider getting bright light every morning by going outside or use a 10,000-lux light box for about 30 minutes. If your low mood persists despite using light, reach out to your healthcare provider.

With good sleep habits and a few small adjustments to your light exposure, your body will settle into the fall time change so you can return to enjoying all the joys of the season.

item.title: Five Ways to Get Ahead of the Upcoming Fall Time Change
item.description:
Sleep

Five Ways to Get Ahead of the Upcoming Fall Time Change

Nervous about the end of Daylight Saving Time? Try these strategies.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Sunday, November 1st, marks the end of Daylight Saving Time and return to Standard Time.
  • Time changes often cause sleep disruption, and the fall time change can be difficult for natural early birds.
  • These five strategies can help you prepare for the seasonal time change and make the adjustment easier.
Source: Cottonbro Studio / Pexels

A time change is fast approaching, and you may be asking yourself, “Is this the one that is easier for me, or the harder one?” In the United States, Daylight Saving Time will end on Sunday, November 1st, at 2:00 am—at which point clocks will “fall back” to 1:00 am, theoretically providing the opportunity for an extra hour of sleep as we return to Standard Time.

Disruptions From the Fall Seasonal Time Change

Although more negative effects are observed during the springtime transition to Daylight Saving Time, both time changes are associated with a temporary increase in sleep disruptions, changes in mood, and even suicide rates. As humans, our bodies like to be on a regular 24-hour cycle, and disruptions—even by one hour—can throw off our circadian rhythms. Although the average person struggles more with the spring transition (when we lose an hour of sleep), the fall transition is typically more difficult for individuals who have an extreme morning-type circadian rhythm. You may be a morning type if you frequently find it difficult to stay up for evening activities, accidentally doze off in the evenings, or wake up earlier than you would like.

Strategies for a Successful Sleep Transition

If you have a history of sleep difficulties or struggle with the end of Daylight Saving Time, there are a few things you can do to make the transition gentler. Here are five strategies to get ahead of the upcoming time change, each supported by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine:

  1. Prioritize good sleep habits. Any time you are at risk of sleep disturbance, it is best to stick to healthy sleep habits, such as avoiding daytime naps, waking up at a consistent time in the morning, and giving yourself adequate wind-down time before trying to sleep. These six healthy sleep habits are based on recommendations from cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) and can help facilitate better sleep throughout a transition.
  2. Start adjusting your bedtime and/or wake-up time several days in advance. If possible, shift your bedtime and wake-up time 15 minutes later each day in the 3-4 days leading up to Sunday. A gradual shift will be less of a shock to your natural circadian rhythm.
  3. Change your clock the night before. Although many of us use phones and digital devices that will automatically update at 2:00 am on November 1st, some devices may allow you to manually set them back one hour on the evening of October 31st. You can also manually change car clocks, kitchen clocks, and analog watches on Saturday evening so that you can go to bed at your (new) normal bedtime and get one day ahead of the transition.
  4. Seek out morning light from Sunday onwards. Exposure to early-morning light can signal your body that it is time for your internal clock to adjust to a new schedule. Get outside in the morning, even for a few minutes—you might also get a mood boost from the crisp autumn air.
  5. Be prepared for kids and pets to take longer to adjust. Despite how well you might cope with the time change, any kids and pets in your house may have more trouble. Use the previous four strategies to support them in the time transition, stay as consistent with schedules as possible, and remember that you will all get through it, as you have each year until now.

If you are struggling with severe sleep difficulties in the days and weeks following the time transition, seek support from a therapist, psychologist, or physician trained in behavioral sleep medicine. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the first-line treatment recommended by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine for individuals with chronic difficulty falling or staying asleep.

item.title: What Really Happens in the Mind When We Experience Déjà Vu
item.description:
Memory

What Really Happens in the Mind When We Experience Déjà Vu

Déjà Vu is more than a "felt before" feeling. It eludes a single explanation.

Posted October 28, 2026

Source: Elias Boberg / Pexels

Have you ever found yourself in a moment so uncannily familiar that it sends shivers down your spine? That eerie feeling of having experienced something before, even when logic insists otherwise.

This phenomenon, known as “déjà vu,” has long eluded psychology and neurology, but research increasingly explores its nature and causes. Research answers some of the questions many have about what déjà vu truly is and why it occurs; however, it requires more explanation.

What Is Déjà Vu?

Echoing its French origins, the term literally translates to “already seen.” Yet, this seemingly straightforward definition belies the experience it encapsulates. Déjà vu transcends visual recognition; it is a phenomenon that spans a spectrum of ‘already’ encounters—heard, met, visited, and more.

In psychology and neurology, déjà vu is not a mere replay of the past; it is a subjective, undefined familiarity, distinct from the genuine recognition of a previously encountered event.

A study published in the Journal of Psychology and Clinical Psychiatry examines the phenomenon's multifaceted nature and elucidates its ‘as if’ quality. In déjà vu, the present experience unfolds with an eerie familiarity, as if echoing a script written in the past. Strikingly, this sensation persists even when, rationally, it never occurred before.

Consider the déjà vu experience as a puzzle piece that doesn’t quite fit into the timeline of memory and perception. It’s not a straightforward memory recall, where one can pinpoint the origin of the familiarity. Instead, it operates in the realm of the ‘as if,’ where the mind grapples with the sensation that the present moment has already unfolded, even though no concrete evidence or memory supports the claim. The ‘as if’ nature adds complexity to the déjà vu experience, challenging our understanding of memory, consciousness, and the intricate configuration of the human mind.

The study’s insights illuminate the elusive nature of déjà vu, prompting us to ponder the brain’s ability to conjure a sense of familiarity that defies conventional explanations. As we unravel the enigma of déjà vu, it becomes clear that this phenomenon is not just a quirk of memory, but a gateway to deeper questions about perception and the mysteries that lie within the recesses of our consciousness.

How Do Psychologists Explain Déjà Vu?

Research in the Journal of Neurology introduces a myriad of psychological theories. Diverse theories are highlighted, such as “mental diplopia,” where the brain splits in déjà vu. From this perspective, déjà vu is proposed to arise from a loss of synchronicity between the brain’s hemispheres, while some propose a simultaneous double perception.

Others argue that déjà vu is almost like a faulty tape recorder within the mind. Perceptions are recorded, and memories are played back, but in déjà vu, the sensory information is recorded and played back at the same time.

From the psychodynamic perspective, Sigmund Freud posited déjà vu as a wish to turn back time, while others see it as a defense mechanism—a psychic reassurance against adversity. Some psychoanalysts even suggest déjà vu as a waking dream or a daytime residue of dreams.

Other theories are outlandish, such as the parapsychological perspective. Déjà vu results from astral teleportation, telepathy, or even memories from past lives, hinting at reincarnation.

Which Perspective Is Correct In Explaining Déjà Vu?

These diverse psychological perspectives on déjà vu imply the multifaceted nature of understanding this intriguing phenomenon. The prevalence of theories on temporal lobe dysfunction—such as mental diplopia or the tape recorder hypothesis—hints at the vast but imperfect network of our cognitive processes, suggesting that déjà vu may not be a singular and straightforward experience, but rather a product of complex interactions within the brain.

Psychodynamic perspectives underscore the emotional underpinnings associated with these experiences, emphasizing deep connections in memory, emotion, and perception. The mention of parapsychological concepts widens the scope, urging us to explore unconventional dimensions and consider the possibility of extrasensory or even metaphysical elements at play in déjà vu.

The amalgamation of these perspectives paints déjà vu as a phenomenon that transcends conventional explanations, asking researchers to delve deeper into the realms of memory and consciousness. However, navigating through these perspectives, it becomes evident that no single theory captures the complexity of déjà vu. Psychologists, neurologists, and even parapsychologists offer intriguing insights, yet the enigma persists.

Despite some consensus on the role of temporal lobe dysfunction, déjà vu defies a singular explanation. The puzzle of déjà vu remains, inviting us to challenge the boundaries of what we know about memory, perception, and the nature of the human mind.

In the vast landscape of psychological inquiry, déjà vu stands as one of many testaments to the mysteries of the human mind. From psychic experiences to intricate neural pathways, the phenomenon remains elusive.

item.title: The Misery of Perfectionism
item.description:
Perfectionism

The Misery of Perfectionism

Perfectionists get it wrong about what they can do and control.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • There are three types of perfectionism, each of which involves overestimating what a person can do or control.
  • Perfectionists are susceptible to grievance when their actual or perceived abilities fall short.
  • Perfectionism leaves people vulnerable to feeling like failures in many aspects of their lives.

Perfectionism can make people miserable. That misery may have a particular character based on the type of perfectionism. There are at least three types, each of which involves overestimation. These are perfectionism as overestimation of

  • Actual abilities
  • Potential abilities
  • How much a person controls the world

These forms can cause a person to have a great deal of resentment and unhappiness in their life. Left unchecked, perfectionism can result in a person harboring huge resentment directed at others. Perfectionism can also result in a person making the judgment that he is a moral failure.

Perfectionism as overestimation of actual abilities

Perfectionists set the bar impossibly high yet operate with the expectation that they will be able to clear it in all their actions. Some people tend to chronically overestimate their abilities while others tend to chronically underestimate theirs.

The underestimators and the overestimators lack perspective on what they can and cannot do. They just plainly get it wrong about their abilities and don’t even know it. That’s self-deception.

Based on inaccurate assessments of their actual abilities, people set their expectations for achievement. If underestimators expect to clear any bar, it must be one set so very low that anyone would trip on it. (This is the opposite of perfectionism that might be called, “Not even good enough.”)

It is the overestimators who are more prone to perfectionism. There is often a significant distance between what we expect ourselves to be able to do and what we are actually able to do. Our expectations may color our assessments, which may tend to widen the already existing gap between actual abilities and expectations.

If that gap is acknowledged even for a bit, the characteristic move to close that gap is to begin to consider our potential abilities, which is another form of perfectionism.

Perfectionism as overestimation of potential abilities

Every person spends some amount of time imagining what it is they might be able to do. Oftentimes, there is a chain of reasoning that runs along like this: I am able to do this, so I will be able to do that because they are similar.

In some cases, this comparison and subsequent conclusion that a person will be able to do that is justified. However, when the types of activities are very different, it becomes more difficult to make good comparisons and draw well-founded conclusions.

Imagine that a person is very good at doing that first activity and has had great success with it. She is able to meet the standards she sets for herself there. When that person tries the new activity, she expects on some level that she will be able to replicate her success. She makes the mistake of assuming that abilities translate across activities, so she overestimates her potential abilities.

This overestimation results in her having skewed expectations that she cannot possibly meet. Yet she expects herself to meet them because she understands herself as a type of person who has met the highest standards before.

Complicating the matter of perfectionism even more is the fact that being able to do something perfectly is not simply a matter of capacity and willingness. Yes, each of these plays an important role, and their absence may make it impossible to accomplish a goal. However, their presence does not guarantee success.

There are all kinds of factors and limiting conditions that have nothing to do with you or me personally that affect our achievement. This leads to the third form of perfectionism.

Perfectionism as overestimation of how much a person controls the world

This is the view that a person should be able to control all factors that affect her activities and achievement. This is another failure of assessment in the direction of overestimation.

Rather than a person’s will, actual abilities, and potential abilities being the site of the mistaken assessment, everything else in the world is the subject of mistaken assessment. More specifically, the perfectionist who believes that she should be able to control all the factors and conditions that contribute to her achievement makes a catastrophic error in judgment.

By expecting to control everything, she puts herself in an impossible situation where there are at least two outcomes. One is that she will resent anything and anyone whom she sees as thwarting her actions and achievements. That resentment may well become toxic. The other option is that she directs her focus inward and makes the judgment that she is a moral failure. Regardless of which path she travels, her agency is deeply compromised.

Perfectionists tend to make themselves the exception to the rules or standards that apply to others.

One strain of perfectionism will manifest in a sense of superiority. These perfectionists tend to think they leave the rest of us behind with no chance of catching up.

The second and more common strain of perfectionism, especially for those of us who struggle with addiction, manifests in blameworthiness, self-recrimination, and inferiority. The inferiority strain often involves overestimators overestimating what they are responsible for.

Taking responsibility for what is not properly yours will lead to more blame and self-recrimination. If we see ourselves as pretty much responsible for everything, including matters well beyond our control, we will always fail. This will reinforce our view that we are worthless.

Turning everything into an obligation

One final dynamic of perfectionism that harms people is turning wants and needs into a series of shoulds and obligations. A perfectionist with a “shoulding” habit turns everything into obligations, which carries the potential for catastrophic failure. It is impossible to meet all the demands created by our goals and wants.

We cannot be in two places at the same time, no matter how much we think we should be able to do so. People struggling with addiction may be especially susceptible to this dynamic because we may believe that in meeting impossible demands, we are atoning for all our past transgressions.

item.title: Not Everything Is About You
item.description:
Anxiety

Not Everything Is About You

Three ways to stop taking things personally

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Noticing others’ emotions doesn’t mean you’re responsible for managing them.
  • Your brain may fill gaps in context with your own insecurities, not facts.
  • Seek clarity through curiosity, not reassurance to relieve your own anxiety.
Source: Yandurkov/Pexels

Why do we immediately assume that someone’s bad mood is about us? Oftentimes, we take a little bit of information or one shift in someone’s behavior and make it about us. We start to replay comments, reread text exchanges, or critically assess what we said and how we said it. It’s exhausting, and most of the time, it’s not warranted.

A new narrative begins to write itself, and suddenly, you are the main culprit. This isn’t ideal, but it makes sense. We are wired to pay attention to details as they pertain to our relationships and interactions. But being aware of how the mood or vibe changes in a room doesn’t mean we need to absorb it all. For a serial fixer, this is often where awareness turns into ownership.

Source: Tara-Winstead/Pexel

When we take bits of information or observations and leave our brains to their own emotional, urgent devices, we can create unnecessary anxiety. Our brains don’t love uncertainty, so when we don't have all the context or information, we begin to fill in the blanks. And of course, the database we have unlimited access to? It’s all about us. Our own experiences, insecurities, and past interactions.

We’ve all been there, in one form or another. Perhaps it’s a colleague who typically comes into the office and greets you with a warm hello, but one morning barely acknowledges you. Within minutes, you’re replaying your last interactions, questioning how quickly you responded to her email yesterday or whether you said something wrong in Monday’s meeting.

You’ve slipped out of the present and are now shuffling through the past while anticipating the discomfort you might feel in the future. Meanwhile, your colleague may have had a challenging morning, and her balloon is already full by 9 a.m. Her behavior may have nothing to do with you, but you’re now spinning, looking for reassurance, and using up valuable energy that could be directed toward the tasks waiting on your to-do list.

For those who tend to struggle with perfectionism, anxiety, or managing others’ emotions, those blanks often get filled with something negative. If you grew up having to be hyperfocused on others’ emotions in an attempt to manage your own discomfort, you may be more prone to scanning the room, noticing every little change, and then taking responsibility for it.

This is a valuable skill, and I’m not suggesting that you disconnect or ignore how our behavior impacts others. The pendulum doesn’t need to swing completely in the opposite direction. It’s about noticing when we’re responding to old patterns and letting past coping techniques become our primary filter for interpreting what’s happening around us.

Hypervigilance or being two steps ahead may have been a necessity in a previous chapter of your life. You might also be operating in a workplace or family culture that fuels urgency, provides little or unclear communication, or leaves you fighting for feedback and affirmation. These environments can leave you filling in the missing pieces and taking ownership of what isn’t yours to carry.

Finding and maintaining that sweet spot between being aware of others’ emotions and deciding what’s yours to carry is challenging, but worth the effort. Your brain will likely continue noticing and interpreting information just as quickly. What we’re working on is how much authority we give those initial interpretations before deciding what to do next.

Eager to get some new kinds of reps in? Here are three ways to insert a little logic to balance out those intense, emotionally driven “what ifs” and help you stay present rather than racing ahead.

Source: Tara-Winstead/Pexels

1. Pause Before Reacting

Practice tolerating the unknown rather than rushing to fix something before you have the facts. Resist the urge to immediately explain, apologize, send another message, or ask what’s wrong. Perhaps you’ve noticed something unusual or received information that feels conflicting. But take a breath. You have some check-in work to do before you take ownership and take action.

Not every uncomfortable observation requires an immediate response. Give yourself permission to sit with a little uncertainty before deciding what, if anything, needs to happen next.

2. Fact-Check Your Story

Be aware of the story you’re telling yourself. What you observed may be accurate, but your interpretation might not be. This involves fighting back against the urge to let one moment or one response override the history of a relationship, whether that history is long or short. Ask yourself,

“What do I know?”

“What evidence do I have?”

“Is this how this person typically communicates or behaves?”

Your initial response isn’t necessarily your most accurate one. You can question it, challenge it, and even change your mind as more information becomes available. You don’t have to treat your first interpretation as the final answer.

3. Seek Clarity, Not Reassurance

Circle back or ask questions that are driven by curiosity, not anxiety. There’s a difference between wanting to understand something and wanting someone else to relieve your discomfort. If you’re primarily looking to be soothed or reassured, give yourself more time to try to find this internally before outsourcing it and perhaps making things more complicated.

This is also where “I statements” can be effective. Share what you’ve observed rather than what you’ve assumed. Beginning with “I’ve noticed...” allows you to open a conversation without assigning blame or jumping to conclusions. For example, “I’ve noticed you’ve been a little quieter than usual. Is everything okay?” opens the door for conversation without immediately making yourself the center of it.

But you might also give yourself some time before asking anything at all. Notice how much real estate the situation takes up in your mind. Does it grow in importance, or does it quickly move in and out of your awareness as you go about your day?

The objective isn’t to be passive or refrain from asking questions. It’s to become more aware of your motives and your timing. Sometimes you may discover that the situation didn’t require your involvement in the first place.

Not everything is about you, and that just might be the most relieving thing you hear all week!

item.title: Can Couples Therapy Make an Abusive Relationship Worse?
item.description:
Domestic Violence

Can Couples Therapy Make an Abusive Relationship Worse?

Most clinicians advise against couples or family therapy for three main reasons.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Couples therapy can give an abusive partner new tools to manipulate or control their victim.
  • Treating abuse as a mutual problem can reinforce victim-blaming and undermine survivors' experiences.
  • When coercive control is present, survivor safety must take priority over relationship repair.

Harris and Adam came to me in the summer of 2025. They had two young children and had just purchased a home. But Adam began to exhibit scary behavior toward his husband, Harris. He had started to yell loudly and had been physically violent a couple of times.

When Adam called me, he hoped therapy could "help" Harris and stop the behavior. In the first session, he asked, "Can you give us some tools to help his behavior?"

Adam's question is common. In cases where children are involved, or other financial or emotional tethers bind couples together, they might consider couples therapy to fix their unhealthy relationship before they think of leaving it. While this approach can help if both partners are willing to work on their own relationship issues, this is usually not the case with an abusive person.

When a relationship involves coercive control or ongoing abuse, couples therapy is generally not recommended because it can reinforce existing power imbalances and potentially place the victim at further risk (Keilholtz and Spencer, 2022). The concern is not simply that a couple has relationship problems, but that the presence of abuse and a power imbalance changes the safety and appropriateness of the therapeutic approach. When I provide training on coercive control, I often advise against couples therapy (in most cases) due to the following three reasons:

  1. Therapy could become part of the coercive control: Suppose the perpetrator’s behavior is brought to light in a therapy session against their will. In that case, the perpetrator can feel vengeful when the couple leaves the safety of the therapist’s office. The power imbalance present in most abusive relationships can put the victim at further risk when entering a therapy space.
  2. Couples therapy can incorrectly frame abuse as a mutual relationship problem: In their need to remain neutral, therapists will often try to get the victim to take on undue responsibility for an abuser’s behavior, suggesting a victim re-evaluate their responses to abuse or that the victim could better manage those reactions. They may even go as far as to suggest they are "provoking" their abuser's behavior, language which, to a victim, is abusive itself.

  3. An abusive partner can manipulate the therapeutic process and further undermine the survivor's reality: Many perpetrators are skilled manipulators (which is often why they can make it so far in the legal system without being caught) and often fool even mental health clinicians. This is why seeking couples therapy in domestic abuse cases may be more harmful to a victim than helpful. A therapist needs to hear both sides and give an unbiased assessment. This too often becomes a critical analysis of a victim’s reactive behavior to abuse instead of addressing the abuse itself.

    If a therapist implies that the victim is equally to blame for reacting to abuse as the abuser is for inflicting it, the victim will absorb this professional assessment as confirmation of all the self-doubt that their abuser has been curating in them. It invalidates the severity of genuine abuse to create a balanced playing field for both partners. This perspective only enhances the abuser’s position of control and revictimizes an already weakened victim.

Source: Geralt / Shutterstock

Unfortunately, with a dangerous partner, deciding to leave is usually easier said than done. This is less about simply leaving and more about making the necessary plans to do so safely. And while it is normal to want to explore all options to help the relationship, especially if kids are involved, it is essential to prioritize safety above all else.
