item.title: Learning to Trust: Discovering Your Authentic Ground
item.description:
Spirituality

Learning to Trust: Discovering Your Authentic Ground

John Prendergast explains the connection between true safety and ego surrender.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • The ego, our sense of being a separate self, is part of our false ground of being.
  • Our true ground is vast, encompassing and embracing. It includes personal, archetypal and universal elements.
  • Spiritual development is not about attaining a state; it's about the search for truth.
  • A deep trust in life is the result of accessing our true ground.
Source: John Prendergast

This is Part Two of a two-part series. Read Part 1 here.

A brilliant outlier in the overlapping fields of depth psychology and spirituality, John J. Prendergast sheds much-needed light on what he calls our “deepest ground.” Bridging Western psychotherapy with the perennial teachings of nondual philosophy, his work as a teacher, writer, and therapist focuses on the powerful process of “waking down,” emphasizing embodied insight—the illumination of emotions, relationships, and ordinary life—as much as transcendental awareness. The author of several books, including Your Deepest Ground: A Guide to Embodied Spirituality and The Deep Heart: Our Portal to Presence, he offers residential retreats in the U.S. and Europe, as well as online workshops and teaching. In this second half of our two-part interview, we talked about the insecurity that arises when we put our trust in the “false ground” of ego, and tools for touching into our spiritual core.

Mark Matousek: You’ve written that many are “deeply confused” about where their “essential safety” lies. This comes from putting their faith in the “false ground” of ego rather than “authentic ground”—if I understand you correctly?

John Prendergast: Yes. The ego is part of this false ground, the conventional way that we take ourselves to be a separate self. I’m in here, you’re out there. I’m this body, and there’s the world (which is not me). Believing ourselves to be the complete agents of our own actions. These positions are part of the common-sense experience of being a separate self.

This experience is accompanied by many levels of contraction that come from identifying with our beliefs, our reactive feelings, and negative somatic responses. All of that is part of what I mean by false ground. Yet when we pay attention, we discover that this is not who we really are, and that can be a very unsettling realization.

MM: How do we free ourselves of identification with this false ground?

JP: It’s helpful to have a practice and also a guide, someone who understands the territory. Having gone through this letting-go process themselves, they’re able to support us in letting go of what we’ve taken to be safe, which means letting go of control. We’re so oriented to trying to be in control in order to be safe. As we relax that tendency toward contraction, we discover that it is actually not safe to live in the manner we have been living. It is a false idea of safety that makes us vigilant, which takes a toll on psychological and physical health. Clinging to false ground makes us stupid, in a way, as well as unresponsive.

Alternatively, the more we live from openness, the deeper our intrinsic trust in life becomes. Such fundamental trust is not that things will work out as we hope and wish, but rather that they will unfold as they need to. That becomes our true ground, our true safety, as experience reveals itself.

This is nothing to do with naivete. We know that this body could become sick. We know we’ll lose our loved ones. We know we’ll die. There’s no denial in this. Instead, there’s a deep embrace of life as it is: the openings and closings, the appearances and disappearances, all of it. That is where true safety comes from.

MM: Many of us are capable of conditional trust, which is based on getting what we want. But the trust you’re describing sounds less personal than that.

JP: It is. And that’s the key distinction: it’s not personal. People associate the word impersonal with coolness or distance or being uncaring. But that’s not it at all. It’s just not egoic. This trust is not concerned with the separate self; in fact, what actually unfolds is freedom from that sense of separation.

MM: In your book, you write about three different kinds of authentic ground. What are they?

JP: The first kind of authentic ground is when we’re in touch with our body. For example, most of us enjoy being in nature. We experience a real appreciation for, and attunement with, physicality and nature. Very often, people who’ve been traumatized don’t have that experience because it was unsafe for them to be in the body. So, the first level of authenticity is actually to enter the body, to feel like it’s safe to be here. A lot of psychotherapy works with that, and with trauma and early attachment issues. That’s good work. I’m very supportive of effective psychotherapy in that regard.

The second level of authenticity is archetypal, and exists largely outside our awareness. There may be flashes of the archetypal realm here and there, during a psychedelic journey or through some other unexpected opening, such as powerful dreams. This is why Jung’s work is so interesting to me. The archetypal level is largely an underground kind of journey. For Jung, there was a descent into this deep underground space that was quite tumultuous in his own life (to the point where he was questioning his own sanity). The archetypal level is where the ancestors live—unredeemed—where ancestral conditioning comes into the psyche and is felt. I’ve sensed this in my own life as well as in my work with clients and mentees. There might be spontaneous memories of pogroms or great-grandparents, images arising from ancestral (or ethnic) streams, waiting to be welcomed into the light of awareness.

Then there’s the universal dimension, what you might call the “groundless ground.” No ancestors, no psychological conditioning, no forms, no categories of description. Instead, the universal dimension is characterized by a deep, dark silence here. There’s no one and nothing there. It’s empty of all form, empty of all thought, full of stillness, silence, and darkness. It’s the emptiness out of which all life comes, welling up from the depths.

As we open to the universal dimension, we begin to feel an essential life emerging, luminosity coming out of the darkness, a song coming out of silence, a dynamic movement coming out of stillness. This is a very, very different quality of life, not dependent on circumstances. Of course, there are traditions that talk about this dimension as well, including Tibetan Buddhism and nondual philosophy, which counsel us to surrender the ego, to open to the life that is moving us all.

MM: It amazes me that waking down—as you describe it—turning to a more holistic approach to self-realization, is not more widely accepted in psycho-spiritual circles.

JP: You do find elements of this teaching in different traditions. My teacher and friend, Adyashanti, has spoken about it but not explicitly (deleted comma) incorporating specific psychological elements. It’s in some of the Tibetan teachings, as I mentioned, as well as in certain contemplative schools, but not with this weaving of depth psychology that I find really important.

MM: To hear a teacher of your stature admit that while you were a skilled meditator, you still needed to go deeper, to pay attention to parts of yourself that you’d missed, is humbling and inspiring. You could have continued in the “transcendent” direction, but chose to focus on waking down, instead.

JP: This is the importance of vulnerability and self-honesty. Those are the most important factors in terms of our spiritual discovery process, in my experience. How much do we really want to know? Are we willing to look at everything? Waking down is not about attaining or sustaining a state or an image. It really comes down to a love for truth. That is what has driven me.

item.title: Hope Is the Light That Shines, Even on the Darkest Day
item.description:
Depression

Hope Is the Light That Shines, Even on the Darkest Day

If you're feeling down, remember you can always get better, so hold on to hope.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • When you're feeling depressed, it's easy to lose hope you will ever get better.
  • That makes sense, because everything can look and feel very negative.
  • But there are many reasons to feel hopeful, because most people recover from depression.
Source: Sankalp Suradkar/Unsplash

We might see depression as some kind of outlier, as if we have the “well” people over here and a separate group, the “unwell” folks, over there. But that’s really not the case. Experiences of psychological distress like chronic anxiety and depression are part of the human condition. They can affect anyone, any time. In fact, I have struggled with both in my life—and depression was a dark cloud hovering over me for much of my 30s and 40s. I have been there, so I know only too well how awful it can feel, how it drains the color out of your days and leaves you feeling overwhelmed, exhausted, and devoid of hope that things will ever get better.

If you’re living with this dark cloud, I’m truly sorry. Dragging yourself through the days is so hard; it’s like walking through quicksand. Your thoughts are probably uncomfortably bleak and very negative, making it hard to see any good in yourself, your life, or your future. Losing hope is the most natural thing in the world. Again, I have been there and felt that, so I understand it with painful clarity.

But please remember there is always hope, even if you can’t feel it right now and the very idea of hoping things will change or improve seems far-fetched, as if someone is saying you could easily run an ultra-marathon. Take it from me, as a therapist who has helped hundreds of people recover from debilitating problems like anxiety and depression. And as someone who lived with depression for many, many years and is now depression-free, apart from normal—and entirely manageable—fluctuations in my mood. Here are three reasons for you to feel hopeful right now.

1. Depression Almost Always Passes With Time

When you’re struggling through a depressive episode, it feels like it will never end, as if you’re in a tunnel with no light up ahead. This is partly because of the way depression affects your mind, skewing your thinking negatively, making you ruminate over and over about all the things that are wrong with you and your life. These circling, painful thoughts focus on everything you ever said or did that was shameful or embarrassing, your perceived mistakes and failures, magnifying even the smallest error into something irrevocable and cringe-inducing.

You may also be trying to numb your painful thoughts and feelings with a substance (alcohol, weed, junk food) or activity (pornography, gaming, spending). And although this is entirely understandable, it doesn’t help. For example, we know that alcohol is a depressant, so the more you drink to numb yourself out, the worse you feel the next day.

It might help to know that, however severe the episode, depression almost always eases over time. I know this through personal experience, as even the most stubborn, hard-to-shift period of depression always passed. And through observing clients who seemed stuck in their low mood, whatever we tried in therapy, until something finally did help, there was a shift, and they began to emerge from the fog. Doing all the right things—therapy, sobriety, meditation, regular exercise, plenty of sleep, and a healthy diet—will help, but even without these positive changes, most depressions usually lift with the passing of time.

2. Neuroplasticity: the Most Hopeful Word I Know

One of my favorite things to teach clients at the beginning of therapy is the concept of neuroplasticity. This is the idea that your brain is plastic, meaning it’s malleable and its neural architecture can change over time. This is a relatively new idea in psychology, as we used to think the brain was largely formed in childhood and adolescence and was then basically set for the rest of a person’s life. Thanks to the miraculous ability of fMRI machines to watch the brain’s activity in real time, we now know this is not true.

Your brain is changing every single day of your life. If you learn something new like, say, Mandarin, your brain needs new structures and pathways to hold all that knowledge. It does this by forging new synaptic connections between neurons and forming new neural pathways, allowing you to think novel, oft-repeated thoughts more quickly and hold all that Mandarin-related information in easily accessible memory networks.

Why is this hopeful? Because it means that, even if you have been struggling with depression your whole life, nothing about these unhelpful thoughts, beliefs, feelings, and behaviors is set in your brain. It can all be changed, with the right help and support. Forging new, more helpful ways of thinking means developing new neural pathways, making use of that miraculous neuroplasticity to shape and mould your brain, through learning something helpful and then repeating it over and over.

For example, change a negative core belief like “I’m a failure” to something more nuanced and realistic, like “I’m not perfect, but nobody is. We all fail sometimes; that’s just part of being human and nothing to be ashamed of.” And for the new belief to take hold, we have to think, speak, or write it over and over until it gets wired into the brain.

That’s why we speak of a meditation or yoga practice, because doing something helpful once makes little impact. But doing it daily for a few months helps wire it in, making it both more effective and easier to do each time.

3. There Is a You Who Is Not Depressed

Let’s add a little internal family systems (IFS) wisdom to this hope-nurturing discussion. In the IFS model, which features various parts of the psyche, such as young, wounded parts and protectors trying to keep them safe, there is another “you” living inside you. This version of you is wise, kind, loving, and nurturing. He or she lives in your heart and mind (well, in your prefrontal cortex if we’re being neuroscientific) and wants nothing but the best for you. This is your self, what Richard Schwartz, founder of IFS, describes as “Who you are deep down.”

And even on the worst, darkest day, your self is not depressed. It’s like the metaphor often used by mindfulness teachers: your depressive thoughts and feelings are like dark, stormy clouds passing across the sky. And your self is the sky, so it is not harmed in any way by the weather, even at its stormiest. And this can be such a helpful, hopeful idea, because knowing there is someone inside who stays balanced, grounded, and robust, while that storm plays itself out, helps you remember you have—perhaps untapped—resources inside to help you recover.

My clients seem to love this idea and resonate with it, even when they are suffering. Knowing there is a way out of that suffering can be life-changing, and in some cases life-saving. I hope it strikes a chord with you too.

And if you are struggling right now, I am sending you warm, healing thoughts and wishes for a swift, lasting recovery.

If you are experiencing depression, especially if you are having suicidal thoughts, please do see your doctor or seek help from a mental-health professional. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: 4 Practical Steps to Build Confidence Without Alcohol
item.description:
Alcoholism

4 Practical Steps to Build Confidence Without Alcohol

Do you borrow confidence from alcohol?

Posted October 28, 2026

One common question I hear: “How do I find the confidence to do these things without alcohol?”

Over the years, we have turned to alcohol for a confidence boost in these and other scenarios:

  • Meeting new people.
  • Showing up for a networking event.
  • Walking up to that attractive person smiling at you across the room.

Without alcohol, it can feel as if we're left to face our vulnerability and self-doubt alone, without our usual armor.

An Invisible Drinking Loop Is the Borrowed-Confidence Loop

Invisible Drinking Loop
Source: Jeanette Hu | Sober Curiosity

For most seasoned drinkers who have eventually come to question their drinking, alcohol is often only what's on the surface. Beneath the drinking patterns, one or more invisible drinking loops usually keep the drinking pattern alive.

When it comes to alcohol and confidence, people often get caught in what I call the borrowed confidence drinking loop. It’s one of the 11 most common drinking loops I see in my work.

In this particular drinking loop, our drinking pattern is driven by our need for self-trust and confidence to go for the things that matter to us, and is fueled by the belief that alcohol can help us boost confidence. Through repetition, drinking becomes our default to quiet fear and self-doubt in situations that require self-trust. Unfortunately, over time, by repeatedly borrowing confidence from alcohol, our own self-trust tends to diminish, rather than grow.

The Borrowed Confidence Drinking Loop
Source: Jeanette Hu | Sober Curiosity

To outgrow these loops, we can learn new skills and tools that allow us to stop turning to alcohol for help. For a borrowed-confidence loop, that means stopping borrowing confidence from alcohol and starting to earn it ourselves. I call this step skill expansion, which is one of the four core pillars of my approach to breaking and growing beyond old drinking patterns.

How do we start to earn confidence without alcohol?

Below are the four practical steps I often share with my clients to help them stop borrowing confidence from alcohol.

Step 1: Mindset Makeover

Real change doesn’t always start with new actions. Sometimes, it starts with a mindset shift.

In modern culture, many of us mistake confidence for a feeling and believe we need to feel confident before we can take action. I call this a limiting mindset—a mindset that holds us back.

Despite modern misconceptions, confidence requires trust and reliance; confidence means taking action despite self-doubt. This is how we earn confidence.

The first step to stop borrowing confidence from alcohol is shifting mindset.

Limiting Mindset: Confidence is a feeling. I need to feel confident before I act.

To Empower Mindset: Confidence is an act of self-trust. When I act despite my self-doubt, I can build confidence.

Step 2: Take a Small Action

Once we shift our mindset, the next step is to put that new belief into practice: choose one small action you can take without borrowing confidence from alcohol.

If talking to new people makes you nervous, make eye contact and smile at someone. If networking events feel intimidating, perhaps show up for 10 minutes without expecting yourself to talk to anyone.

The goal isn't to feel completely comfortable or doubt-free, or even to get a certain kind of result. It's to allow yourself to act despite feeling uncomfortable.

Step 3: Celebrate the Action

After taking that small action, give yourself credit for doing it.

Many of us judge ourselves based on outcomes. But when it comes to building confidence, the outcome isn't the most important part. What matters is that we were willing to take action despite our self-doubt. And here are two secrets that many people don’t realize:

  • Secret 1: You are unlikely to get the “ideal” result when you're just starting to practice something new.

But that is perfectly okay, because:

  • Secret 2: It’s the action, not the result, that helps us build confidence and self-trust.

Instead of asking yourself, 'Did I do well?' ask, 'Did I show up and take action despite my self-doubt?' If the answer is yes, then it’s time to celebrate.

Step 4: Assess, Adjust, then Repeat

Once you've celebrated the action, it’s time to assess the result.

  • If you liked the result, what worked that you want to repeat?
  • If you didn’t like the result, what could you adjust next time?

Getting the result you want in one try isn't the goal. We can keep learning, adjusting, and giving yourself opportunities to try again. And it’s through this process that confidence is built.

Beyond the Borrowed Confidence Drinking Loop

Building confidence without alcohol is an essential step toward breaking a borrowed confidence drinking loop. But addressing a single loop is rarely enough to break an unwanted drinking pattern.

That's because many unhealthy relationships with alcohol are maintained not just by one drinking loop, but by multiple loops that overlap and interact across different areas and situations in our lives.

That's why identifying the different loops that keep our drinking patterns alive is often the first step toward truly breaking them.

item.title: How Gen Z Men Are Building Meaningful Friendships
item.description:
Friends

How Gen Z Men Are Building Meaningful Friendships

Hinge leverages NBA star Jared McCain’s friendship with Nate to inspire male connection.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Over 70% of Gen Z men say vulnerability is essential or very important in friendship.
  • Shared activities are a common starting point for close friendships among Gen Z men.
  • Humor and vulnerability can coexist as meaningful ways men show up for one another.

Recent research has examined factors that impact men’s social connection. Findings suggest that while men often connect through shared activities like work and sports, traditional masculinity norms emphasizing self-reliance and invulnerability can make it more difficult to sustain these connections (Nordin et al., 2024).

Against this backdrop, Hinge conducted a cross-sectional survey of 2,587 U.S. Gen Z adults to explore how men build, value, and struggle with close friendships. The data informed the creation of the One More Hour, an impact initiative designed to foster real-life connection, one hour at a time.

I connected with Moe Ari Brown (he/they), Love and Connection Expert at Hinge, to discuss what people misunderstand about vulnerability in male friendships and how these findings can inform building meaningful friendships as an adult.

Vulnerability in Male Relationships

Data from Hinge’s study demonstrate that vulnerability may actually be a friendship standard for Gen Z men. While over 57% of Gen Z men shared that their fear of being vulnerable has gotten in the way of getting closer to people, 71% report that a willingness to be vulnerable is essential or very important in friendship.

In fact, men are actively looking for more ways to connect. “Our culture often misinterprets a lack of male friendship as a lack of desire for male friendship. It's not necessarily that men struggle to be vulnerable once they're in a friendship; the challenge lies in the process of building that friendship in the first place,” states Moe.

Research similarly suggests that men vary in how they seek and use social support. McKenzie and colleagues (2018) found diverse patterns of connection, challenging assumptions that men are uniformly less interested in building emotionally supportive relationships.

This highlights that male loneliness may be less about how men show up in their relationships and more about whether they have friendships to show up in at all.

The most commonly cited barriers to men developing close relationships included:

  • Social anxiety (66%);
  • Not knowing if the feeling is mutual (66%);
  • Not knowing where to find potential friends (64%); and
  • Difficulty fitting it into their schedules (62%).

According to Moe, “Vulnerability isn't always a big, emotional heart-to-heart. Sometimes it's allowing yourself to have a friend, letting someone check on you, talking about your day, or making space for another person in your routine. Even sending a meme, responding to a text, or consistently showing up for someone requires a willingness to care and be cared for.”

Source: Courtesy of Hinge

Building Meaningful Friendships

Making friends as an adult can feel uniquely hard, as many built-in opportunities for connection go away over time.

Nearly half (47%) of Gen Z men said their close friendships usually start by participating in the same activities, such as playing sports or gaming. A majority of these men view having shared hobbies as a marker of close friendship.

Accordingly, Moe shares the following advice:

  • Start with the places and activities you're already drawn to, like the gym, a recreational sports league, a gaming community, or another hobby.
  • Don't put too much pressure on yourself to build a meaningful friendship right away.
  • Start by learning someone's name, striking up a conversation, or suggesting an activity you can do together.

Research supports the importance of spending time together. Hall (2019) found that greater time spent together was associated with closer friendships, with leisure activities particularly important for developing closeness.

Actionable Friendship Tips

Moe also shared some actionable steps for building friendships. They highlight that some of the most meaningful ways we show up for one another happen in ordinary, everyday moments:

  1. Start small: If you're looking to make new friends, begin with a simple conversation. Say hello to someone you see regularly or connect over a shared interest.
  2. Make time for shared activities: Friendship doesn't always need to revolve around serious conversations. Go to a game, grab coffee, play basketball, or spend time doing something you both enjoy.
  3. Check in on the little things: Send a funny meme, ask how a friend's job interview went, or follow up after a first date. These gestures communicate that you're thinking about them.
  4. Pay attention when something feels off: If a friend who is usually active in the group chat goes quiet or starts missing regular plans, reach out. A simple check-in can go a long way.
  5. Offer support without waiting to be asked: Instead of asking a friend if they need help, let them know you'd genuinely like to be there for them.
  6. Create consistency: Establish a weekly check-in, standing coffee date, or monthly activity. Regular touchpoints help friendships grow stronger over time.
Source: Courtesy of Hinge

The Friendship of Jared and Nate

NBA star Jared McCain and Nate Thai are best friends. The duo talks openly about how their mix of humor and vulnerability has sustained their friendship. Their friendship serves as a model for How We Friend, part of the One More Hour campaign that showcases the small, often unseen moments that strengthen male friendships.

The initiative highlights real-life examples, like the difficult moment in Jared’s basketball career when he tore his meniscus, to highlight what showing up for each other looks like. According to Jared:

"He [Nate] was there for me when I first got injured. It was me and him in Philly. When I got injured, I didn't know what to do. I've never not had basketball to fall back on. He was the one to crack the first joke. When I first got the call that I tore my meniscus, the first thing he said to me was, ‘At least you have another leg,’ which I love. It's such a Nate comment to make. And from then on, he helped me. I couldn't leave my bed for a while, and he was there for me."

Nate shares his own version of this stage of their relationship:

"I was joking with him, trying to make it all funny. But when it came down to it, I sat him down and we talked. I told him it’s going to be good. I was just there for him, making sure he knows the injury isn’t the end of his journey. He still has a long journey ahead of him. His career’s not over. Whether it was basketball or off the court, his life was going to be good regardless. It was going to work out."

Data from Hinge’s study highlight that male friendships are not just about jokes. In fact, half of Gen Z men in the U.S. report that conversations with their close friends are an even mix of surface-level and emotionally deep.

When asked about balancing jokes with making space for what’s really going on in his friendship with Nate, Jared shared:

"It's kind of a joke online that they [men] don't talk about their feelings or how they actually feel. They don't dive deep into more questions about what they want out of this life. But that's huge in terms of a real, honest friendship. Me and [my best friend] Nate, we troll all the time. But we both know if we need to have a serious conversation, we'll get serious and we can be vulnerable with each other. That's huge for male friendships, in general. People find it hard to get vulnerable with certain issues they're having mentally, emotionally, whatever it is going on. But I think me and Nate do a really good job of handling that and knowing how to tackle any issues with each other."

When I asked Moe what he has learned from the lived experiences of people like Jared and Nate, he shared that their friendship is “a beautiful example of how humor, paired with vulnerability, can build brotherhood. Whether you call it brotherhood, chosen family, or friendship, every guy I’ve ever met just wants to know that he is enough and that he belongs somewhere, just as he is.
